newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy 1996 trade surplus seen up on 1995 -report.
newsitem.headline: Italy 1996 trade surplus seen up on 1995 -report.

text.p: Italy's 1996 trade surplus is likely to exceed the 1995 level by over 10 trillion lire, or 0.5 percent of GDP, a report by JP Morgan Milan said.

"On a balance of payments basis, this would put the annual trade surplus at a record-high 4.4 percent of GDP," the report said, adding Italy's current account surplus is expected to rise to around three percent of GDP this year, sharply up from 2.3 percent last year.
Italy posted a 1995 trade surplus of 25.18 trillion lire.

"Italy's trade performance this year has been impressive," the report said, noting the surplus in the first eight months of the year was 11.9 trillion lire up on the same 1995 period, although the pace of improvement was expected to moderate in the final months of 1996.

JP Morgan said it expected further trade improvement in 1997, although the recent lira appreciation and ERM re-entry "beg the question of how competitive and sustainable the current level of the currency is.
"We think that, against the core European currencies, the lira is at a sustainable level...Against the dollar the lira looks overvalued, but that is a problem common to Europe as a whole," it said.
Despite the higher currency, the report said, net exports will continue to benefit from relative demand conditions.
"We reckon Italy's trade balance is much more sensitive to the relative growth performance (vis-a-vis Italy's main trading partners) than it is to changes in relative prices.
"We expect Italy's growth to remain significantly below the European average next year, and probably into 1998 as well, due mainly to a more severe degree of fiscal tightening.
"This should ensure continued improvement in both the trade and current account surpluses," the report added.
JP Morgan forecast Italian GDP growth of 0.8 percent in 1996 and 1.2 percent in 1997, against a forecast average European growth of 1.5 percent in 1996 and 2.5 percent in 1997.
